typescript-fundamentals-sr1-07.reason: ambiguous: the unqualified 'one-parameter function fits a two-parameter slot' is false when the first parameter types differ. Now concrete, with matching first parameters (tsc 7.0.2 accepts it). (final: keep)
typescript-fundamentals-sr1-07.statement: `(a: number) => void` is assignable to the type `(a: number, b: string) => void`.
typescript-fundamentals-sr1-07.explanation: A function may ignore extra arguments, so a source with fewer parameters fits a target with more, provided each of its parameters matches the target parameter in the same position.

typescript-fundamentals-sr1-09.reason: ambiguous: 'satisfies a return type' reads as an annotated function returning a fresh literal, which gets an excess property error. Now tests function-type assignability with a non-fresh source (tsc 7.0.2 accepts it). (final: keep)
typescript-fundamentals-sr1-09.statement: Given `let f = () => ({ a: 1, b: 2 })`, TypeScript accepts assigning `f` to a `() => { a: number }` variable.
typescript-fundamentals-sr1-09.explanation: TypeScript requires the source function's return type to be a subtype of the target's, and `{ a: number; b: number }` has every member that `{ a: number }` needs.

typescript-fundamentals-sr1-05.reason: tell: error words (rejects, reports, fails) marked only true statements. Same fact (readonly is ignored in compatibility) and same answer, false. (final: keep)
typescript-fundamentals-sr1-05.statement: TypeScript rejects assigning a `{ readonly x: number }` value to a variable of type `{ x: number }`.
typescript-fundamentals-sr1-05.explanation: TypeScript ignores `readonly` when comparing object property compatibility. An alias with a mutable property may therefore change the same object.
typescript-fundamentals-sr1-05.misconception: The readonly modifier makes structurally identical object types assignment-incompatible.

typescript-fundamentals-sr2-08.reason: explanation_error: the strictNullChecks qualifier implied that void would be assignable to number with the flag off (tsc6 and tsc 7.0.2 reject it either way). The qualifier is gone, and the statement avoids the 'A value of type X is assignable to Y' false template, which already carries sr2-02 and sr2-05. (final: keep)
typescript-fundamentals-sr2-08.statement: TypeScript accepts `let n: number = done()` when `done` has the return type `void`.
typescript-fundamentals-sr2-08.explanation: Apart from `void` itself, a `void` value is assignable only to `any` and `unknown`, whatever the `strictNullChecks` setting, so a void call result is unusable as a number.
typescript-fundamentals-sr2-08.misconception: A void result can be assigned to a concrete value type such as number.

typescript-fundamentals-sr3-02.statement: TypeScript flags `n` as implicit `any` in `xs.map(n => n.toFixed())` for `xs: number[]`.
typescript-fundamentals-sr3-02.explanation: The callback sits where the signature of `map` supplies a contextual type, so TypeScript infers `n` as `number` and `noImplicitAny` has nothing to report.
typescript-fundamentals-sr3-02.misconception: Unannotated callback parameters fall back to implicit any.

typescript-fundamentals-sr3-04.explanation: A `const` binding only stops reassignment of `opts`. Its properties stay writable, so TypeScript widens the literal `3` to `number`.

typescript-fundamentals-sr4-02.reason: tell: transformation verbs (removes, changes, converts) marked false statements. Now uses the 'narrows to' form of the true narrowing cards. Same fact (typeof 'object' keeps null) and same answer, false. (final: keep)

typescript-fundamentals-sr4-02.explanation: `typeof null` evaluates to `'object'`, so TypeScript retains `null` in the guarded branch.

typescript-fundamentals-sr4-03.reason: ambiguous: 'still processes the empty string' is false at runtime but true at type level. Now asks only what the checker narrows to; tsc 7.0.2 keeps string | null in the falsy branch. (final: keep)

typescript-fundamentals-sr4-03.explanation: The empty string is falsy too, so TypeScript keeps `string | null` in the falsy branch. That is why a truthiness check on a string can skip `""`.
typescript-fundamentals-sr4-03.misconception: A falsy check on a nullable string leaves only null.

typescript-fundamentals-sr4-07.reason: ambiguous: the checker's instanceof narrowing filters union members structurally, so 'by property names' was defensible. typescript-fundamentals-sr4-07.statement: For `class Foo { id = 1 }` and `const f: Foo = { id: 2 }`, `f instanceof Foo` is `true`.
typescript-fundamentals-sr4-07.explanation: `instanceof` checks whether `Foo.prototype` is on the prototype chain of `f`, so the plain object literal fails it, even though TypeScript accepts it as a `Foo` by its shape.
typescript-fundamentals-sr4-07.misconception: A value the checker accepts as a class type is an instance of that class at runtime.

typescript-fundamentals-sr5-08.reason: ambiguous: 'can extend one other interface at a time' is literally true. Now states the false limit outright, as the verifier suggested; Object Types says interfaces 'can also extend from multiple types' and shows ColorfulCircle. (final: keep)

typescript-fundamentals-sr7-08.explanation: Each interpolated union is cross multiplied with the others, so two two-member unions give four strings: `"a-1" | "a-2" | "b-1" | "b-2"`.
typescript-fundamentals-sr7-08.misconception: Template literal types zip union members by their positions.
